implementation_notes: The TypeScript answer: model the node set as a discriminated union (a literal kind/type field on each variant) and write each operation as a function whose switch narrows the variant; a final assertNever (or `const _x: never = node`) turns a forgotten variant into a compile error. No accept() is needed, the nodes stay plain data, and because the type system is erased at run time the discriminant must exist in the data. Keep the class-based visitor when the elements are classes whose behaviour must stay cohesive, when operations must be enumerable by reflection-like tooling, or when the hierarchy predates the union refactor - the class form gives the same completeness guarantee through `implements`.
pitfalls: The never check only protects functions that use it: a switch without a default that falls through (or a function whose return type admits undefined) quietly returns undefined at run time.
Discriminants must be literal-typed; widening kind to string or typing the value as a supertype disables narrowing and with it the exhaustiveness proof.
Type assertions (as Shape) and non-null assertions opt out of narrowing and are the usual way the guarantee is lost in real code.
Structural typing accepts any object that happens to fit the union, so never rely on class identity or on the value having been built by your constructors.

variants.name: Class-based accept() / visit() visitor with a Visitor interface
variants.idiom_name: abstract Element with accept<R>(visitor) and a Visitor interface per operation
variants.implementation_notes: The literal OO translation: an abstract Shape with accept<R>(visitor: ShapeVisitor<R>): R, concrete elements whose accept calls visitor.visitThis(this), and a ShapeVisitor interface with one method per element class. Declaring a class that implements ShapeVisitor forces every method, so completeness is checked by the type system exactly as the never-check does for the union form, and the generic R keeps visitors returning values instead of mutating shared state. Choose it when element classes genuinely own behaviour, when operations must be injectable objects (dependency injection, fake visitors in tests), or when a class hierarchy already exists and the accept hook is cheaper than reshaping the data into a union.
pitfalls: A subclass that forgets to override accept inherits the base implementation and dispatches the wrong visit method; make accept abstract and test each element against each visitor.
Class instances do not survive a JSON round-trip, so instanceof-based dispatch (and accept) breaks on deserialised data - rehydrate through constructors first.

A visitor whose methods return R forces every method to produce a value; visitors that only accumulate state should use void and keep state on the instance, which then cannot be shared across concurrent traversals.

The generic parameter on accept makes the interface awkward for operations with different result types sharing one visitor; split the visitor interface per result type instead of widening R to unknown.
